nameStory: Red valerian gets its name from its clusters of vibrant red to pink flowers that bloom abundantly throughout the growing season. The name 'valerian' comes from the Latin 'valere' meaning 'to be strong,' referring to the plant's hardy nature and ability to thrive in challenging conditions like rocky walls and poor soils.
description: Red valerian is a showy perennial herb that forms bushy clumps 2-3 feet tall and wide. It produces dense, rounded clusters of small tubular flowers in shades of red, pink, or occasionally white that sit atop sturdy stems. The plant has blue-green, lance-shaped leaves that grow in opposite pairs along the stems. Originally from the Mediterranean, it's primarily found as an ornamental garden plant that sometimes escapes cultivation in New England.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense, rounded clusters of tiny tubular flowers, typically bright red to deep pink, each flower less than half an inch long with a sweet, honey-like fragrance that attracts butterflies

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Blue-green to gray-green leaves arranged in opposite pairs, lance-shaped and smooth-edged, with a slightly waxy feel and no leaf stalks - they attach directly to the stem

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms bushy, upright clumps 2-3 feet tall with multiple branching stems that feel somewhat succulent and break easily when bent

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, dry seeds each topped with a feathery white plume that helps them blow in the wind, appearing in late summer after flowers fade

habitat: In New England, red valerian is most commonly found in cultivated gardens, particularly rock gardens and perennial borders. It occasionally escapes to grow wild along stone walls, in rocky areas, or disturbed soils near residential areas. The plant thrives in well-drained, alkaline soils and full sun locations.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as blue-green shoots from the base, with flowering beginning in late spring as dense clusters of buds form at stem tips.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with showy red-pink flower clusters that continue opening throughout the summer months, attracting numerous butterflies and moths.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and develop into fluffy seed heads that disperse in autumn winds, while leaves may persist until hard frost.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, leaving only dried stems and seed heads that may persist into winter before breaking down.

funFact: Red valerian is sometimes called 'kiss-me-quick' because its sweet nectar is so irresistible to butterflies that they practically dive into the flower clusters, and the flowers are edible for humans too - they taste mildly sweet and peppery, making a colorful addition to salads!
confusionNotes: Red valerian might be confused with garden phlox, but valerian's flowers are much smaller and more densely packed, and its leaves are blue-green and directly attached to the stem rather than phlox's bright green stalked leaves. Memory trick: valerian's leaves are 'value-packed' right onto the stem with no stalks.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name, red valerian is not closely related to true valerian (Valeriana officinalis), the herb used for sleep aids - they're in the same plant family but different genera. Red valerian is purely ornamental and doesn't have the medicinal properties or strong smell of true valerian.
compareHints: Red valerian is the only Centranthus species commonly found in New England gardens. Within the honeysuckle family, it differs from actual honeysuckles by growing as an upright herb rather than a climbing vine, and from elderberries by having much smaller individual flowers in denser, more rounded clusters rather than large flat-topped flower heads.
